author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
My first attempt in writing a philosophy essay collaborating with AI.  Other than my engineering degree, I minored in philosophy.

My approach writing this essay is me and GPT dialogue on a topic over multiple days, kind of like Socrates having a dialogue with random people on the street of Athens.   Then I ask GPT to turn it into an undergrad level philosophy essay, revise the draft a little bit more.   Then I ask GPT to draw a cover image, revise it a little bit too.

Here is the essay.   If the reaction is good, I am planning to start a new series on AI philosophy.  Not philosophy of AI, but use AI to do philosophy.

comments.text: I love it and look forward to reading more articles if you end up doing more. I took an undergraduate art class while I was working on my math and computer science degree. One thing we discussed in class was "What is art? What is the definition of art?" I think the definition we were taught was along the lines of "Art is anything that makes you (a person) feel a certain way." You touched on this in your essay - "A critic might respond that artistic judgment is different because art is essentially human. Art expresses consciousness, emotion, intention, spirit, or cultural meaning. Therefore only a conscious being can truly understand it." And then you talked about how chess engines objectively evaluate chess positions. Is a chess position art? I think so. I watch a lot of chess streamers and study a lot of games, and some positions are described as being "beautiful." When a chess engine analyzes a position, it's much more black and white (figuratively). Positions are evaluated as winning or losing, not as being beautiful or not. I absolutely think that AI-generated art is a form of art. What I am not sold on is whether an AI can actually "know" art, because AI does not "feel." Thanks for the thought provoking article.
